name: Red House

dates.note: The list entry gives the single year 1859. The node's exemplar note says 'Built 1859-60'; the Wikipedia article says the house was co-designed in 1859 and construction was completed in 1860. All are recorded; none is resolved.

quotes.text: 1859. By Philip Webb (his first commission) for William Morris, who lived here until 1864. Moderately sized L-shaped building, of 2 storeys. Picturesque design in the simplified Gothic style of Street and Butterfield's domestic work. Red brick, with hipped tiled roof. Gabled, 2 storeyed, porch to north front. Oriel to west lighting main room on first floor. Staircase tower in angle, with pointed roof and finials.
quotes.page: Official list entry, Details section, paragraph 2 (List Entry Number 1064203).

quotes.text: Sliding sash windows, singly and in pairs, with cambered heads beneath relieving arches. Casements with leaded lights of circular form to upper floor. Interior almost unaltered. Important fixed cupboards, settle and other furnishings with some painted decoration by Burne-Jones and others.

note: Tranche 3, British picturesque and Arts and Crafts cluster, 5 Sep 2026. The register's reading contradicts the node's on the point the node cares most about. The node's prose says Red House had 'no style label available to describe it' and that it is where the English tradition 'stops copying periods and starts studying construction'; Historic England calls it a 'Picturesque design in the simplified Gothic style of Street and Butterfield's domestic work' -- that is, a label, and the same label the corpus's own `gothic-revival-british` node carries. The entry also records sliding sashes on the ground floor and leaded casements above, which is the mixed fenestration the node's own note describes as 'sash and casement windows of different shapes placed where the rooms wanted them'.
